transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/time: 2026-12-18 08:00 PT (16:00Z)
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Mike (DataBeam CTO), Jenna (SRE), Ravi (ML Eng), Ava (Product), Chris (Security)

Summary: quick scoping for POC benchmarks and harness integration. Focus areas: workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming behavior, load test harness, success criteria (latency/throughput/cost), and timelines. Lots of notes about warm up, KV cache, quantization variants.

Topics:
- Representative scripts and traffic traces
- Load testing methodology (concurrency, batching, token-level vs request-level metrics)
- Streaming response impact on tput and SLOs
- Bench harness integration (Jenkins or internal runner vs Redwood harness)
- Success criteria and go/no-go thresholds
- Security and KMS/SSO constraints

Transcript: 
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanna make sure we scope the benchmark so it maps to the real workload, not just synthetic tokens. mike, can you kick off with a quick description of the user flows you care about?
[00:18] Mike (DataBeam): yeah thanks, so primary is our chat assistant for customer support, most requests are short, 20-70 tokens output, some longer summary jobs 400-800 tokens but those are <5% of traffic. typical concurrency is variable, peak around 2000 active users but concurrent inference requests we expect something like 150-300 reqs/s in peak. also we have streaming enabled in prod for chat, so we care about streaming latency p95 and also end-to-end completion time.
[00:45] Jenna (SRE): and to add, from infra side we want p95 under 200ms for short replies and p95 under 1.5s for long summaries, otherwise user experience drops. cost target is roughly $X per 1M tokens but we'll refine once we see the numbers.
[01:05] Samir: ok great. lina, from benchmark perspective what do we need from customer?
[01:12] Lina (Redwood SE): two things: first, the actual inference scripts you run in prod or a close mimic, second, a 24-72 hour traffic trace with timestamps so we can replay realistic arrival patterns. for harnesses we can either plug your scripts into our runner or we can give a lightweight harness you run in your infra to capture telemetry. note: if you run locally we need stable env variables and a warmup protocol so cache/KV warming is fair.
[01:40] Ravi (ML Eng): question: when you say streaming harness, does that mean you replay token-level streaming, latencies per token, or just measure first-byte and end-of-stream?
[01:50] Lina: good call. we recommend token-level metrics: first-byte latency, per-token delta, and completion time. streaming changes resource patterns - it's heavier on scheduler and more sensitive to small latencies, so our runner includes a streaming emulation mode. but if your scripts aren't instrumented for per-token timestamps, we'll fall back to first-byte + completion.
[02:15] Mike: our current client uses SSE and flushes every token chunk, we can instrument it to emit token timestamps, should be doable.
[02:25] Ava (Product): also want to ensure the benchmark exercises fallback rules - e.g. fall back from our preferred low-cost model to a higher-latency high-cost model during stress, we need to measure that behavior.
[02:40] Samir: yep we can simulate routing policies, make sure rollbacks and fallbacks are exercised. ok let's talk success criteria, what are the must-haves?
[02:53] Jenna: must have: p95 latency for short responses <= 200ms, p99 < 350ms. throughput >= 250 reqs/s sustained for 10 minutes under steady state. CPU/GPU utilization should not exceed 85% in steady state to allow headroom. also error rate < 0.1% and no dropped streams.
[03:18] Ravi: and for accuracy success we want no more than 2% change in quality compared to our current baseline model - we'll provide eval prompts.
[03:28] Samir: good. lina, when you run the harness what variants will you test?
[03:33] Lina: we typically run: 1) hosted default model (baseline), 2) quantized variant (8-bit or 4-bit depending on model support), 3) larger model fallback, 4) streaming vs non-streaming mode. each run includes warmup period (10-15 mins) to populate prefix/KV cache and then an at-scale run for 10-30 minutes. we'll collect p50/p95/p99 token latencies, requests/s, GPU util, mem, and tail latencies per inference.
[04:00] Chris (Security): on the private/KMS front: we need to ensure keys never leave our KMS, the logs sent to Redwood cannot contain PII, and audit logs must be kept for 90 days. can you confirm your private deployment supports HSM-backed keys?
[04:18] Samir: yes for Redwood Private we support customer KMS/HSM integrations and logs can be filtered client-side. we'll send the SOC2 + iso docs this week.
[04:27] Mike: about load generation, our traffic is spiky - do you support replaying bursty patterns and diurnal cycles?
[04:35] Lina: absolutely, we can ingest your trace and replay at scale; our harness supports scaling arrival rate and maintaining request inter-arrival timings. for extreme spikes we recommend a hybrid test: replay with preserved arrival times plus a uniform stress run to check worst-case saturation.
[04:57] Ravi: another thing - our in-house scripts batch small groups of messages into single requests sometimes. how do you emulate batching?
[05:05] Lina: you can provide the batching logic in the script and our runner will execute it. or we can parameterize batch-size and simulate micro-batches. batching will change per-token costs and latency tradeoffs. we'll capture batch sizes and effective token/s.
[05:20] Samir: we should capture both token-level cost and per-request cost so we can show unit economics.
[05:26] Jenna: how about warmup: is there a recommended cache-warmup pattern?
[05:31] Lina: yes, we recommend a progressive warmup: 5-10 minutes at 10% traffic, then 2x, then to 100% to let KV cache and model kernels settle. also run the same prompts used in production so prefix caches reflect reality. avoid synthetic single-token warmups which don't reflect real prompt distributions.
[05:52] Mike: good point. on instrumentation side what metrics do you need from us?
[05:58] Lina: token counts, per-token latency (if available), request-level latencies, concurrency, GPU util, memory, and any application-level retries. logs with request ids help correlate traces.
[06:12] Ava: timeline? how long for initial benchmark and then POC?
[06:16] Samir: typical timeline: first week - onboarding + provide scripts and traces; week 2 - harness integration and initial runs; week 3 - remediation and additional runs; week 4 - composite report and recommendations. so a 3-4 week POC with an initial pilot run in week 2. for you we can accelerate if Ravi can drop scripts this week.
[06:38] Ravi: I can drop two scripts and a 48-hour trace by Tue (2026-12-22).
[06:44] Samir: perfect. lina, on the streaming vs non-streaming tests how do you compare cost?
[06:50] Lina: streaming can increase scheduler overhead and slightly reduce throughput per GPU because of smaller per-request batching opportunities. cost model: we report tokens/s and tokens-per-dollar under each mode. often streaming increases cost by ~5-20% depending on chunking frequency. we'll quantify it with your exact chunk size.
[07:12] Mike: we chunk every 32 tokens, sometimes 1 token flush on punctuation, so might be on the higher side.
[07:20] Jenna: any concerns around tokenization differences across models?
[07:24] Lina: yes ensure you provide the exact tokenizer and model config; different models' tokenization will change token counts and thus cost. we normalize to tokens-per-1k-requests as well as tokens-per-1M for cost.
[07:39] Samir: security note: when we run hosted benchmarks we can do them in a dedicated tenant with logs scrubbed; for Private we can run in your VPC. which do you prefer for initial runs?
[07:51] Chris: prefer initial runs in Redwood hosted dedicated tenant with scrubbed logs, then Private evaluation for final verification. we need the scrub rules documented.
[07:59] Samir: we'll include scrub rules in the runbook.
[08:04] Ravi: about benchmark harness - can the harness run on our k8s cluster to keep network path realistic?
[08:09] Lina: yes, we have a lightweight runner that you can deploy as a POD, it reports telemetry to the Redwood dashboard or writes to a local S3 compatible store. if you want full isolation, run the harness in your VPC and we can pull anonymized metrics.
[08:26] Mike: ok good. what about measuring p99 tail latencies for streaming? those are super spiky.
[08:32] Lina: we'll collect per-request per-token timing and report p50/p95/p99 and also tail distribution graphs. for streaming we'll show first-byte and last-byte latencies and per-token deltas. also we'll surface outliers with connected traces.
[08:49] Jenna: expected artifacts from Redwood after a run?
[08:52] Samir: runnable report with graphs for latency and throughput, a CSV of raw samples, cost projection table (tokens, costs), and suggested configuration changes (batch sizes, quantization, route policies). we'll also include a short replayable harness config for reruns.
[09:08] Ava: about quantization - how do you test quality regressions?
[09:12] Lina: we run automated eval prompts you provide across baseline and quantized variants and compute delta in pass@k or BLEU-ish measures depending on task; for chat we look at response coherence via a small eval set and flag any >2% degradation. also we can run human spot checks if needed.
[09:33] Ravi: any gotchas with batching + streaming?
[09:36] Lina: yes typically batching is less effective with heavy streaming because you can't buffer tokens long enough; micro-batches help but increase latency. our harness will test combinations: streaming+microbatch(x), non-streaming+batch(y) and show the tradeoffs.
[09:55] Mike: what's the expected footprint on GPUs? we run on A100 and have older V100s for cheaper lanes.
[10:01] Lina: we'll report GPU mem and compute usage. quantized variants reduce memory and allow larger batch sizes; some kernels favor A100 for speed. if you want, we can run the same workload on both GPU types to show delta.
[10:16] Samir: let's capture acceptance criteria again so everyone's aligned.
[10:20] Jenna: acceptance: p95 short responses <=200ms, sustained throughput >=250 reqs/s for 10 minutes, error rate <0.1%, cost delta within agreed threshold, and quality regression <2%.
[10:33] Samir: good. next steps recap: samir will send runbook + sample harness, ravy will upload scripts and traces by 12/22, lina to craft streaming vs non-streaming test plan and load script, security will review KMS/HSM docs. schedule pilot run week of 12/28.
[10:56] Mike: any blockers on Redwood side?
[10:58] Samir: just getting the scripts and access. also confirm whether you want hosted dedicated or private.
[11:05] Chris: start with hosted dedicated scrubbed logs then private for final.
[11:09] Samir: perfect. we'll follow up with calendar invite for 12/28 and share the runbook by 12/20. thanks everyone.
[11:18] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: automated captions, occasional mis-attributions (e.g., RAvI sometimes labeled Ravi ), some filler words removed.
